opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the more underrated uses of these models. A base model, before you've done any post-training on it, has basically learned to imitate the whole distribution of people who write things on the internet. So in some sense it's a compressed model of a huge population of humans, with all their different viewpoints, writing styles, and ways of reasoning. If you prompt it the right way, you can sample from different parts of that distribution. You can say, here's a person with this background, these beliefs, living in this place, how would they answer this survey question? And you get something that's at least somewhat correlated with how real people would answer.

What excites me is that social science has always been bottlenecked on running experiments. Surveys are expensive, field experiments are slow, and a lot of the questions you'd like to ask you can't ethically or practically test on real people. If you had a reasonably faithful simulator, you could do a lot of cheap exploration first. You could pilot a survey, try a thousand variants of the question wording, see which effects seem robust, and then go confirm the interesting ones with actual humans. It's a bit like how physicists use simulation to decide which experiments are worth running.

There's also an interesting angle on the models themselves. Post-training, RLHF and so on, tends to collapse the model toward one persona, the helpful assistant. You lose a lot of the diversity that was in the base model. So the base model is in some ways a more honest mirror of the population, and studying how well it reproduces known findings tells you something about what it has actually learned about people.

That said, I'd be cautious. The internet isn't a representative sample of humanity, and the models have their own quirks and biases, so you can't just treat the outputs as ground truth. I think the right framing is hypothesis generation, not replacing real studies. But as a tool for making social science faster and more iterative, I think there's a lot of potential that people haven't fully tapped yet.

r002.rationale: It explicitly proposes studying how well the base model reproduces known findings, in the context of social science.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that gets me excited is that a base model, before you do any RLHF on it, is basically a model of the whole distribution of human text. It hasn't been collapsed into a single persona yet. So when you prompt it, you're not talking to one character, you're sampling from this enormous population of possible writers, with all their different beliefs and styles and incentives. That's a pretty remarkable object to have if you care about how people think and behave in aggregate.

The classical problem in social science is that experiments are expensive and slow. You want to know how people respond to a message, or how a norm spreads through a group, or how a negotiation plays out under different conditions, and you have to recruit participants, pay them, worry about them figuring out what you're testing. With a base model you can run thousands of these simulations in an afternoon, vary one thing at a time, and look at the whole distribution of outcomes rather than a single sample. You get something closer to a wind tunnel for social dynamics.

Now, I want to be careful here, because the obvious objection is that it's not actually people. It's a model of text people wrote, which is a biased slice of what people think. So I don't believe you should take the numbers at face value. The way I think about it is more as a hypothesis generator. You run the simulation, you see some surprising effect, and that tells you where to point a real study. And you can calibrate: run the model on experiments where we already know the answer from the human literature, see where it agrees and where it fails, and that gives you a sense of which kinds of questions it's trustworthy on.

The other thing I find interesting is that the base model is useful precisely because it hasn't been trained to be agreeable. A chat model wants to give you the answer you're looking for. The base model will happily simulate someone who's wrong, or stubborn, or acting in bad faith, because those people exist in the training data. For social science that's a feature, because a lot of what you want to study is exactly that friction between people with different views.

So there's a real tension there with how we usually think about alignment. We spend most of our effort making the model into a single helpful assistant, and this is a case where the raw, unshaped model is the more valuable scientific instrument. I think that's a reminder that these models are more than just chatbots. They're a compressed representation of a lot of human experience, and we've barely started figuring out what you can learn by querying that directly.

r001.rationale: The candidate proposes simulating social dynamics and examining outcome distributions, but does not describe using questionnaires or conversations to investigate correlations among human traits.

r002.rationale: The candidate proposes running the model on experiments with known results from the human literature and checking where it agrees or fails.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that a base model has this enormous repertoire of human behavior. It hasn’t been trained just to be a helpful assistant—it can continue a conversation, an argument, or a story from lots of different perspectives. So you can potentially use it to simulate people interacting and see what kinds of patterns emerge.

You could study how information spreads through a group, or how people arrive at a consensus, and vary the conditions much more easily than you could with real people. The big question is whether you’re learning something about human behavior or just about the model’s expectations of how a story like that should go. I’d want to start with experiments where we already know the human results and see whether the simulations reproduce them, including how the results change when you change the setup. If that works, then you have a pretty interesting tool for generating hypotheses.

r001.rationale: It proposes simulating people interacting and studying group patterns such as information spread and consensus, but does not mention questionnaires or investigating correlations among human traits.

r002.rationale: It proposes starting with experiments where human results are already known and checking whether simulations reproduce them as the setup changes.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that a base model has learned something about a huge range of people and situations, and you can try to draw out those different behaviors through prompting. You can describe a situation, give it a character to play, and see what happens when you change the incentives or the information that character has.

The big question is whether you’re learning something about people or just about the model. If you ask it to simulate an experiment, it might reproduce the result because it has read about that experiment. That’s much less interesting than predicting what would happen in a new situation.

So I’d want to test it on experiments where we have human data, ideally data the model hasn’t seen, and see which effects it gets right. If that works even within a limited domain, you could use it to explore hypotheses and design better experiments before running them with people. That seems like a pretty exciting tool.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prompting a model to simulate characters in situations, but does not propose using questionnaires or conversations to investigate correlations among human traits.

r002.rationale: It proposes checking whether the model reproduces experimental results, including testing on human data from experiments the model may not have seen.
